passages.source_text: αὐτίκα γοῦν ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ φωνῇ τοῦ νόμου φαίνεται καὶ ἑαυτῷ αὐτοὺς ὁμοίους λέγων. οὕτως γὰρ γέγραπται ὡς ὅτι τῷ πρώτῳ ἀνθρώπῳ, ἐντολὴν ἔχοντι παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀπὸ παντὸς ξύλου τοῦ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ φαγεῖν, ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ξύλου τοῦ γινώσκειν καλὸν καὶ πονηρὸν μὴ φαγεῖν, ὁ ὄφις διὰ τῆς γυναικὸς ἐπὶ ὑποσχέσει τοῦ γενέσθαι αὐτοὺς θεοὺς φαγεῖν αὐτοὺς πείσας, ἀναβλέψαι ἐποίησεν καὶ εἶθ᾽ οὕτως ὁ θεὸς ἀναβλέψασιν αὐτοῖς ἔφη „ἰδοὺ γέγονεν Ἀδὰμ ὡς εἷς ἐξ ἡμῶν“. ὁ μὲν οὖν ὄφις εἰπὼν „ἔσεσθε ὡς θεοὶ“ ὡς ὄντων θεῶν εἰρηκὼς φαίνεται ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ἢ καὶ θεὸς ἐπεμαρτύρησεν εἰπὼν „ἰδοὺ γέγονεν Ἀδὰμ ὡς εἷς ἐξ ἡμῶν“. οὕτως ὁ τοὺς πολλοὺς εἰπὼν ὄφις εἶναι θεοὺς οὐκ ἐψεύσατο. πάλιν τὸ γεγράφθαι „θεοὺς οὐ κακολογήσεις καὶ ἄρχοντας τοῦ λαοῦ σου οὐ κακῶς ἐρεῖς“ πολλοὺς σημαίνει θεούς, οὓς οὐδὲ κακολογεῖσθαι θέλει. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλοθί που γέγραπται „εἰ ἐτόλμησεν θεὸς ἕτερος εἰσελθεῖν καὶ λαβεῖν ἑαυτῷ ἔθνος ἐκ μέσου ἔθνους ὡς ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ θεός“. τὸ εἰπεῖν „εἰ ἐτόλμησεν θεὸς ἕτερος“ ὡς ὄντων ἑτέρων εἴρηκεν. καὶ ἄλλοτε „θεοὶ οἳ τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν [οὐκ ἐποίησαν, ἀπολέσθωσαν“ ὡς τῶν] μὴ πεποιηκότων ἀπόλλυσθαι μελλόντων. καὶ ἄλλη που λέγει „ἔπεχε σεαυτῷ, μὴ πορευθεὶς λατρεύσῃς θεοῖς ἑτέροις, οἷς οὐκ ᾔδεισαν οἱ πατέρες σου“, ὡς ὄντων θεῶν ἑτέρων, οἷς καὶ μὴ ἐξακολουθεῖν αὐτοὺς λέγει. καὶ πάλιν „ὀνόματα θεῶν ἑτέρων οὐκ ἀναβήσεται ἐπὶ τῶν χειλέων σου“. καὶ ἐνταῦθα πολλοὺς θεοὺς λέγει, ὧν τὰ ὀνόματα ὀνομάζεσθαι οὐ θέλει. καὶ πάλιν γέγραπται „κύριος ὁ θεός σου, οὗτος θεὸς τῶν θεῶν“. καὶ πάλιν „τίς ὅμοιός σοι, κύριε, ἐν θεοῖς;“ καὶ πάλιν „θεὸς θεῶν κύριος“. καὶ πάλιν „ὁ θεὸς ἔστη ἐν συναγωγῇ θεῶν, ἐν μέσῳ δὲ θεοὺς διακρίνει“. ὅθεν θαυμάζω πῶς τοσούτων φωνῶν ἐγγράφως μαρτυρουσῶν πολλοὺς εἶναι θεούς, οὐ διαβεβαιοῦσαι μὴ δεῖν μήτε λέγειν μήτε εἶναι νομίζειν. λοιπὸν πρὸς τὰ σαφῶς ῥηθέντα εἴ τι ἔχεις εἰπεῖν, ἐπὶ πάντων λέγε.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Συντομώτερον ἄκουε πρὸς ἃ εἴρηκας. αὐτὸς ὁ νόμος ὁ πολλάκις εἰπὼν θεοὺς αὐτὸς τῷ Ἰουδαίῳ ὄχλῳ λέγει „ἰδοὺ κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ σου ὁ οὐρανὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ πάντα ὅσα ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτοῖς“, συνπεριλαβὼν ὅτι εἰ καὶ εἰσὶν θεοί, ὑπ’ αὐτόν εἰσιν, τουτέστιν ὑπὸ τὸν Ἰουδαίων θεόν. καὶ πάλιν „ὅτι κύριος ὁ θεός σου, οὗτος θεὸς ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἄνω καὶ ἐν τῇ γῇ κάτω, καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλος πλὴν αὐτοῦ“. καὶ ἄλλη που λέγει ἡ γραφὴ τῷ Ἰουδαίων ὄχλῳ „κύριος ὁ θεός σου, οὗτος θεὸς τῶν θεῶν“, ὥσπερ ὅτι εἰ καὶ εἰσὶν θεοί, ὑπὸ τὸν Ἰουδαίων θεόν εἰσιν. καὶ ἄλλη που περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγει ἡ γραφὴ „ὁ θεὸς ὁ μέγας καὶ ἀληθινός, ὃς οὐ λαμβάνει πρόσωπον οὐδὲ μὴ λάβῃ δῶρον, ποιῶν κρίσιν ὀρφανῷ καὶ χήρᾳ“. „μέγαν“ δὲ καὶ „ἀληθινὸν“ καὶ „κρίσιν ποιοῦντα“ τὸν Ἰουδαίων ἡ γραφὴ εἰποῦσα θεὸν τοὺς ἄλλους μικροὺς καὶ οὐκ ἀληθινοὺς ἐσήμανεν. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλη που λέγει ἡ γραφὴ „ζῶ ἐγώ, λέγει κύριος, οὐκ ἔστιν θεὸς ἕτερος πλὴν ἐμοῦ. ἐγὼ πρῶτος, ἐγὼ μετὰ ταῦτα, πλὴν ἐμοῦ θεὸς οὐκ ἔστιν“. καὶ πάλιν „κύριον τὸν θεόν σου φοβηθήσῃ καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις“. καὶ πάλιν „ἄκουε, Ἰσραήλ, κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστίν“. καὶ ὁμῶς πολλαὶ φωναὶ μεθ’ ὅρκου ἐπισφραγίζουσιν ὅτι εἷς ἐστὶν ὁ θεὸς καὶ πλὴν αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἔστιν θεός. ὅθεν θαυμάζω πῶς τοσούτων μαρτυρουσῶν φωνῶν ἕνα εἶναι θεόν, σὺ πολλοὺς εἶναι λέγεις.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ὁ λόγος τὴν ἀρχὴν ἦν μοι πρὸς σὲ ἀπὸ γραφῶν ἐλέγξαι σε ὅτι ψεύδῃ λέγων μὴ πολλοὺς δεῖν φθέγγεσθαι θεούς. ὅθεν πολλὰς ἐγγράφους ἔδειξα φωνὰς ὅτι αὐταὶ αἱ θεῖαι γραφαὶ πολλοὺς φθέγγονται θεούς. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Αὐταὶ αἱ πολλοὺς φθεγγόμεναι θεοὺς γραφαί, αὐταὶ παρήγεσαν ἡμῖν εἰποῦσαι „ὀνόματα θεῶν ἑτέρων οὐκ ἀναβήσεται ἐπὶ τῶν χειλέων σου“. οὕτως οὐ παρὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον ἔφην, ὦ Σίμων. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ἄκουσον πρὸς αὐτὸ καὶ σύ, ὦ Πέτρε. ἁμαρτάνειν μοι δοκεῖς ὅτι αὐτῶν καταλέγεις, τῆς γραφῆς λεγούσης „οὐ κακολογήσεις, καὶ ἄρχοντα τοῦ λαοῦ σου οὐ κακῶς ἐρεῖς“. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Οὐχ ἁμαρτάνω, Σίμων, ἀκολούθως ταῖς γραφαῖς τὴν ἀπώλειαν αὐτῶν προσημαίνων· οὕτω γὰρ γέγραπται· „θεοὶ οἱ τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν οὐκ ἐποίησαν, ἀπολέσθωσαν“, καὶ τοῦτο εἰπὼν οὐχ ὡς ἐνίων πεποιηκότων καὶ μὴ ἀπολλυμένων, ὡς ἡρμήνευσας. δηλοῦται γὰρ εἷς ὁ πεποιηκὼς τῷ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς γεγράφθαι „ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν“. καὶ οὐκ εἶπεν „οἱ θεοί“. καὶ ἄλλη που λέγει „ποίησιν δὲ χειρῶν αὐτοῦ ἀναγγέλλει τὸ στερέωμα“. καὶ ἐν ἑτέρῳ τόπῳ γέγραπται „οἱ οὐρανοὶ αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμενεῖς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα“.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Πρὸς τὸ ἐμὲ δεῖξαι πολλοὺς εἶναι θεοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν φωνὰς σαφεῖς παρέστησα, σὺ δὲ τοσαύτας ἢ καὶ πλείονας φωνὰς ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν γραφῶν ἐνήνοχας, δεικνύων ὅτι εἷς ἐστὶν θεὸς καὶ οὗτος Ἰουδαίων. καὶ πρὸς τὸ εἰπεῖν με „οὐ δεῖ κακολογεῖν θεοὺς“ ἐπήγαγες πρὸς τὸ δεῖξαι ὅτι εἷς ἐστὶν ὁ πεποιηκώς, ὅτι οἱ μὴ πεποιηκότες ἀπολέσθαι ἔχουσιν. πρὸς δὲ τὸ εἰπεῖν με ὅτι δεῖ θεοὺς λέγειν, καθὸ καὶ αἱ γραφαὶ αὐτοὺς λέγουσιν, καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο ἔδειξας ὅτι μὴ δεῖ αὐτῶν ὀνόματα φθέγγεσθαι, τῷ τὴν αὐτὴν γραφὴν εἰπεῖν ὀνόματα θεῶν ἑτέρων μὴ φθέγγεσθαι. ἐπεὶ οὖν αὐταὶ αἱ γραφαὶ πολλοὺς λέγουσιν εἶναι θεοὺς καὶ ἄλλοτε ἕνα μόνον εἶναι — καὶ ὁτὲ μὲν μὴ κακολογεῖσθαι, ὁτὲ δὲ κακολογεῖσθαι: πρὸς τοῦτο τί δεῖ λογίσασθαι ἢ ὅτι αὐταὶ ἡμᾶς αἱ γραφαὶ πλανῶσιν;

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Οὐ πλανῶσιν, ἀλλ’ ἐλέγχουσιν, καὶ εἰς φανερὸν ἄγουσιν τὴν ἐν ἑκάστῳ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνδομυχοῦσαν ὥσπερ ὄφεως κακὴν προαίρεσιν. πολλοῖς γὰρ καὶ διαφόροις τύποις ἐοικυῖαι πρόκεινται. ἕκαστος οὖν κηρῷ ἐοικυῖαν τὴν αὐτοῦ προαίρεσιν ἔχων, περιβλεψάμενος αὐτὰς καὶ πάντα εὑρὼν ἐν αὐταῖς, ὁποῖον θεὸν εἶναι θέλει, τὴν (ὡς ἔφην) κηρῷ ἐοικυῖαν προαίρεσιν ἐπιβαλὼν ἀπομάσσεται. ἐπεὶ οὖν ὅ,τι ἂν βούληταί τις περὶ θεοῦ φρονεῖν, ἐν αὐταῖς εὑρίσκει, τούτου χάριν ὁ μὲν πολλῶν θεῶν ἰδέας ἀπομάσσεται ἀπ’ αὐτῶν, καὶ ἡμεῖς τὴν τοῦ ὄντως ὄντος ἀπεμαξάμεθα ἰδέαν, ἐκ τῆς ἡμετέρας μορφῆς τὸν ἀληθῆ ἐπιγνόντες τύπον. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ ἔνδοθεν ἡμῶν ψυχὴ τὴν αὐτοῦ εἰκόνα πρὸς ἀθανασίαν ἠμφίεσται. ταύτης τὸν γεννήτορα ἐὰν καταλίπω, δικαίᾳ κρίσει καὶ αὐτή με καταλιπεῖν ἔχει (αὐτῷ τῷ τολμήματι γνωρίσασα ἄδικον) καὶ ὡς ἀπὸ δικαίου δικαίως καταλείψει με, καὶ οὕτως τὴν ψυχὴν μετὰ κόλασιν, τῆς ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἀπολειφθείσης βοηθείας, φθαρήσομαι. εἰ δὲ ἔστιν ἕτερος, πρῶτον ἐνδυσάτω ἑτέραν ἰδέαν, ἑτέραν μορφήν, ἵνα διὰ τῆς τοῦ σώματος καινῆς μορφῆς τὸν καινὸν ἐπιγνῶ θεόν. εἰ δὲ καὶ τὴν μορφὴν ἀλλάξει, μήτι καὶ τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν οὐσίαν; εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀλλάξει, οὐκέτι ἐγὼ εἰμι, ἄλλος γενόμενος καὶ μορφῇ καὶ οὐσίᾳ. ἄλλους οὖν πλαττέτω, εἰ ἄλλος ἐστίν. οὐκ ἔστιν δέ. εἰ δὲ ἦν, ἔπλασεν ἄν. ἐπεὶ οὖν οὐκ ἔπλασεν, ὡς οὐκ ὢν τὸν ὄντα τῷ ὄντι καταλιπέτω. οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἔστιν ἢ μόνῃ γνώμῃ. Σίμωνος. ἐγὼ ἄλλον θεὸν οὐ παραδέχομαι πλὴν τὸν κτίσαντά με μόνον.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`

passages.text: ‘Indeed, in the law's first utterance he even appears to speak of them as like himself. For it is written that the first human had received God's command to eat from every tree in the garden, but not to eat from the tree of knowing good and evil. The serpent, through the woman, persuaded them to eat on the promise that they would become gods, and caused them to see. Then, when they had come to see, God said to them, “Look, Adam has become like one of us.” Thus the serpent, saying, “You will be like gods,” appears to have spoken as though gods exist, all the more so since God too testified, saying, “Look, Adam has become like one of us.” So the serpent, who said that there are many gods, did not lie. Again, the writing, “You shall not speak evil of gods, and you shall not speak badly of the rulers of your people,” indicates many gods, of whom he does not even wish evil to be spoken. Elsewhere too it is written, “Has another god dared to go in and take for himself a nation from the midst of a nation, as I, the Lord God, have?” In saying, “Has another god dared,” he spoke as though others exist. And elsewhere, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish,” as those who did not make them are going to perish. Somewhere else it says, “Watch yourself, lest you go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,” as though other gods exist, whom he also tells them not to follow. And again, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” Here too he speaks of many gods, whose names he does not wish to be named. Again it is written, “The Lord your God, he is God of gods.” And again, “Who is like you, Lord, among gods?” And again, “God of gods, the Lord.” And again, “God stood in an assembly of gods, and in their midst he judges gods.” So I wonder how, when so many utterances testify in writing that there are many gods, you do not firmly assert that one must neither call them gods nor believe that they exist. For the rest, if you have anything to say in response to these clear statements, speak before everyone.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean look up or regain sight. The ensuing Adam quotation and the related form ἀναβλέψασιν support their coming to sight or awareness here; opened their eyes is an idiomatic alternative but supplies an unexpressed anatomical object.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ἢ καὶ θεὸς ἐπεμαρτύρησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: all the more so since God too testified
lexical_decisions.rationale: The awkward comparative sequence is read as reinforcing the serpent's statement with God's corroboration. More literally, all the more in this respect—or even God testified. The main text makes the evidentiary link intelligible without changing who speaks or testifies.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ διαβεβαιοῦσαι μὴ δεῖν μήτε λέγειν μήτε εἶναι νομίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: you do not firmly assert that one must neither call them gods nor believe that they exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the printed οὐ and the subsequent prohibition's negatives are retained. The resulting question is rhetorically awkward in Simon's argument; the initial negative is not silently deleted or changed into a different Greek word to resolve the difficulty.
The quoted Greek title is translated Lord, not replaced by Yahweh, since this is the wording quoted by the ancient author rather than a fresh translation from a Hebrew divine-name occurrence.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘Hear a briefer reply to what you have said. The law itself, which has often spoken of gods, itself says to the Jewish multitude, “Look, to the Lord your God belong the heaven of heaven and everything in them.” This includes the point that, even if gods exist, they are under him, that is, under the God of the Jews. Again, “For the Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other besides him.” Somewhere else scripture says to the Jewish multitude, “The Lord your God, he is God of gods,” as though to say that even if gods exist, they are under the God of the Jews. Elsewhere scripture says of him, “The great and true God, who shows no partiality and will accept no gift, rendering justice to orphan and widow.” In calling the God of the Jews great, true, and one who renders justice, scripture indicated that the others are small and not true. Elsewhere too scripture says, “As I live, says the Lord, there is no other god besides me. I am first; I am after these things; besides me there is no god.” Again, “You shall fear the Lord your God and worship him alone.” And again, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord.” Indeed, many utterances seal with an oath that God is one and that there is no god besides him. So I wonder how, when so many utterances testify that there is one God, you say there are many.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: the heaven of heaven and everything in them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular heaven of heaven and the ensuing plural pronoun are preserved as quoted, rather than harmonized with a different scriptural form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ λαμβάνει πρόσωπον οὐδὲ μὴ λάβῃ δῶρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: shows no partiality and will accept no gift
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first idiom concerns favoritism rather than literally taking a face. The second names a gift in a judicial context, where bribe is a plausible explanatory alternative; the main wording keeps the source's expressed noun.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I am first; I am after these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied expression after these things is translated rather than replaced with the familiar but unprinted title last.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Lord your God is one Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: The quoted word order permits the traditional one-Lord rendering or the Lord is one. The main rendering keeps the repeated Lord and the explicit numerical one, without importing a different creed or Hebrew wording.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘My argument with you from the beginning was to expose you from the scriptures as lying when you say one must not speak of many gods. That is why I showed many written utterances: the divine scriptures themselves speak of many gods.’ Peter said, ‘The very scriptures that speak of many gods also instructed us, saying, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” So I did not speak against what is written, Simon.’ Simon said, ‘Listen to a reply to that too, Peter. You seem to me to sin in speaking against them, since scripture says, “You shall not speak evil, and you shall not speak badly of a ruler of your people.”’ Peter said, ‘I do not sin, Simon, in foretelling their destruction in agreement with the scriptures. For it is written, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish.” This does not mean, as you interpreted it, that some did make them and will not perish. For the maker is shown to be one by what is written from the beginning: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” It did not say “the gods.” Somewhere else it says, “The firmament announces the work of his hands.” And in another place it is written, “The heavens themselves will perish, but you will remain forever.”’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb presents the scriptures as providing the instruction that follows. They appeared before us is a more spatially literal alternative; the argument treats their quoted prohibition as the operative instruction.
The term denotes the established heavenly expanse in the quoted cosmological language. It is not modernized into a scientifically specified atmosphere or an otherwise unexpressed material dome.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘To show that there are many gods, I presented clear utterances from the scriptures. You have brought as many, or even more, utterances from those same scriptures to show that there is one God, the God of the Jews. In answer to my saying that one must not speak evil of gods, you added, to show that there is one maker, that those who did not make must perish. In answer to my saying that one must speak of gods, since the scriptures also speak of them, you showed that one must not utter their names, because the same scripture says not to utter the names of other gods. Since, then, the scriptures themselves speak of many gods and at other times of only one, and sometimes say not to speak evil of them and at other times to speak evil of them, what must we conclude from this except that the scriptures themselves mislead us?’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The question is about the inference required by the stated premises, retaining the necessity expressed by δεῖ rather than substituting mere ability.
The term means leading astray or deceiving, not merely presenting a neutral diversity of views. Its accusation is retained as Simon's argument.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘They do not mislead; they expose, bringing into the open the evil intention against God that lurks like a serpent within each person. For they lie before us resembling many different impressions. Each person, having his own intention like wax, looks over them and finds everything in them. Whatever kind of god he wants to exist, he presses upon them his intention, which, as I said, resembles wax, and takes its impression. Since, then, anyone finds in them whatever he wishes to think about God, one person takes impressions of many gods from them. We, however, have taken the image of the one who truly exists, recognizing the true impression from our own form. Moreover, the soul within us is clothed in his image for immortality. If I abandon the begetter of this image, it too must abandon me by a just judgment, recognizing me as unjust from that very act of audacity. Coming from a just one, it will justly abandon me, and thus I shall perish in soul after punishment, when the help from it has departed. If there is another god, let him first clothe me in another appearance, another form, so that through the body's new form I may recognize the new god. But even if he changes the form, will he also change the soul's substance? If he changes that too, I am no longer myself, having become another in both form and substance. Let him therefore fashion others, if there is another. But there is not. If there were, he would have fashioned them. Since he has not fashioned them, being nonexistent, let him leave the one who truly exists alone. For there is no such one except in Simon's opinion alone. I accept no other God besides the one who created me.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The scriptures' differing patterns are likened to forms that stamp wax. Impressions keeps the molding image that develops in the verbs of pressing and taking an imprint; types or models are lexical alternatives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτης τὸν γεννήτορα ἐὰν καταλίπω, δικαίᾳ κρίσει καὶ αὐτή με καταλιπεῖν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: If I abandon the begetter of this image, it too must abandon me by a just judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronouns are read as referring to the immediately preceding image in which the soul is clothed. The soul itself is a grammatically possible alternative, but the ensuing loss of assistance and destruction as to the soul favors the protecting image as what departs.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἀπὸ δικαίου δικαίως καταλείψει με
lexical_decisions.chosen: Coming from a just one, it will justly abandon me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase from a just one is read as the image's provenance from the righteous creator. A more literal alternative is and, as from a just one, it will justly abandon me; the main text does not make the unjust person just in order to remove the tension.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ψυχὴν μετὰ κόλασιν, τῆς ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἀπολειφθείσης βοηθείας, φθαρήσομαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I shall perish in soul after punishment, when the help from it has departed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative soul is taken as the respect in which destruction occurs, and it continues the image as the help's source. This conditional destruction is not softened into bodily death alone or harmonized with the later description of souls as immortal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἔστιν ἢ μόνῃ γνώμῃ. Σίμωνος
lexical_decisions.chosen: For there is no such one except in Simon's opinion alone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative concerns the proposed other god. The genitive Simon's completes opinion across the printed punctuation; no second speaker or missing sentence is invented.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
